notes: hand-curated fallback (E4, must-include): pipeline found only 1 usable-strength battle(s) under general_id='subutai' (need 4); using data/generals.csv's gold-set row verbatim. Scope limited to battles where Subutai (Sube'etei) held personal supreme command or joint co-equal command with Jebe, applying this dataset's established 'personally supreme-commanded' bar (already used to exclude Genghis Khan's Irtysh River/Parwan, Saladin's al-Babein, Frederick's Kesselsdorf, Napoleon's Auerstedt, Grant's Corinth, and Zhukov's Stalingrad/Kursk/Bagration). Net roster is 5 rows -- Battle of Khunan (1222), Battle of Khankala (1222), Battle of the Kalka River (1223), Battle of Mohi (1241), Siege of Kaifeng (1232-33) -- the thinnest roster in this dataset alongside Scipio Africanus (5) and a deliberate research finding, not a shortcut: Subutai spent most of his 50-year career as a senior subordinate commander under Genghis Khan, then Ogedei, then Batu, and the great majority of his most famous campaigns fail either the personal-command bar or the no-fabricated-numbers bar on closer sourcing. Excluded on the personal-command bar (someone else held the specific battle's named field command, even though Subutai contributed forces or planning to the same campaign): the 1216-1219 Merkit pursuit campaign (Chem River) -- Christopher Atwood credits Jochi with supreme command, Subutai leading only a subordinate contingent, the same 'Irtysh River' pattern already excluded from Genghis Khan's own roster; the Siege of Kolomna (1238) -- Wikipedia's own battle-specific infobox names Burundai and Kulkan as commanders and does not list Subutai at all, despite secondary campaign-level summaries placing him with the invasion force, a materially weaker individual attribution than this dataset requires; the Battle of the Sit River (1238) -- field command held by Burundai; the Battle of Legnica (1241) -- commanded by princes Baidar and Kaidan on a separate front from Subutai's own column, with Subutai credited only with prior planning guidance to Baidar's detachment; the Siege of Nishapur (1221) -- commanded by Tolui, Subutai operating elsewhere in Persia/Azerbaijan by that point in the Khwarazmian pursuit; the Sack of Ryazan (1237) -- individual command attribution weaker than Kolomna's, most summaries crediting Batu directly. Also excluded on a genuine, unresolved command-attribution dispute rather than a clean subordinate-command case: the Battle of Sanfengshan (Feb 1232), the decisive field battle that destroyed the Jin's last army immediately before the Kaifeng row above -- Wikipedia's own battle-specific article credits Tolui as tactical planner (Ogedei present) and does not mention Subutai, while Subutai's own biographical literature (Gabriel's book-length framing especially) credits him as the tactical author; without a source giving Subutai direct, specific personal command the way the Yuan Shi does for Mohi below, this is treated as excludable per the same strict standard used for Zhukov's Stavka-coordinator battles -- flagged here since it is the closest call in this roster and a strong tactical case exists for including it. Also excluded, same reason: the Battle of Daohuigu (Nov 1230-Jan 1231), Subutai's one credible personal defeat candidate (a costly Mongol repulse at Tongguan Pass, 'more than 10,000 soldiers and tens of thousands of horses' lost in Mongol chronicles) -- command is split between Tolui's first phase and a second phase credited to Subutai, and the one hard casualty figure found is not clearly attributable to Subutai's specific phase rather than Tolui's; including it risked crediting or debiting Subutai for losses that may not be his. As a consequence this roster has no losses (5 wins), not because Subutai's real record was flawless -- Daohuigu is a real, well-documented personal setback in his career -- but because the one candidate defeat with real numbers failed this dataset's attribution-integrity bar specifically, the mirror image of how Zhukov's roster includes Operation Mars as a real loss precisely because that one is cleanly attributed. Excluded on the no-fabrication bar (real, notable engagements with no quantifiable troop-strength or casualty figure for one or both sides in any source found, the same bar used for Alexander's Persian Gate, Genghis's Khalakhaljid Sands, Saladin's Marj Ayyun, Hannibal's Nola battles, and Scipio's Great Plains): the Battle of the Irghiz River (1219, engagement broken off at nightfall before a real battle developed, no casualties in any source and an unresolved, wildly divergent troop-strength range depending on which of two disputed dates -- 1209 or 1219 -- a source assumes); the Battle of Sagim/Sagimi (1221, an earlier, less-documented Georgia engagement, only qualitatively 'massacred', no numbers); the Battle of Samara Bend (1223, Volga Bulgaria -- command itself is unresolved between Subutai, Jebe, and Jochi, and troop strength is flatly 'unknown' on both sides; one primary account suggests this may actually have been a rare Mongol defeat, but with no numbers to anchor a row either way); and the 1220 Jebe/Subutai pursuit of Muhammad II through Rayy, Qazvin, and Hamadan (a chevauchee of city-sacking, not a discrete two-sided pitched battle -- no troop count for the opposing side or a casualty figure for any single engagement survives, only qualitative destruction language for the sacked cities as a whole; the Kalka River row already captures this same reconnaissance-in-force campaign's culmination). era=Medieval and tech_era_tier=2 for every row, matching Genghis Khan and Saladin, the dataset's other Medieval-era generals -- Subutai's entire personal-command career fell within Genghis Khan's reign and the regencies/khanates of his immediate successors, the same stirrup-cavalry, pre-gunpowder-artillery technology basis (the Kaifeng row's Jin thunder-crash bombs were a defensive weapon used against the Mongols, not part of the Mongol army's own arsenal, so it does not change this general's own tech tier). resource_backing_tier is set per-row (2 for the 1222-1223 Caucasus/Kalka reconnaissance-in-force, cut off from home-base resupply and operating on what the force could forage; 4 for Mohi, part of the empire-scale western campaign under Ogedei's direct authorization; 5 for Kaifeng, the converged main imperial siege army under the reigning Great Khan's direct command before Subutai assumed sole authority) -- same per-row approach as Frederick, Napoleon, and Grant elsewhere in this dataset. Net record is 5 wins, 0 losses (see the Daohuigu exclusion above for why -- not a claim of an undefeated career, a data-attribution-integrity limitation of this specific roster).
